I have run this meeting maybe forty times, and I always start the same way. Before anybody talks about people, we list the packages on one page. Twelve packages, fifteen, sometimes thirty on a large plant. Then we put one name next to each one, and that part is usually quick, because everybody knows what their office is good at. The slow part is the third column, which is the interfaces. For every package I ask the same question: who is on the other side of this line, and when are the two of you going to talk? If nobody answers, I do not close the meeting. Last month we split a plant with a team in Brazil, and we spent twenty minutes on the packages and an hour and a half on the interfaces. That is the right proportion.

In my experience a joint project almost never fails inside a package. It fails at the joint. I will give you the example I use with every new engineer. Two offices split a plant. One takes the building, the other takes the equipment. Both are excellent. Six months later, at the handover, we discover that the building team designed the foundation for a machine that the equipment team changed in March, and nobody told them, because the change was inside their scope. Technically they were both right. Commercially we lost eleven weeks. Since then I put one person on each interface, on both sides, and they talk every two weeks whether there is news or not. It looks like a waste of time until the first time it saves you.
